subject: Fit meausures using sam function with multiple imputation (mitml)

messages.author: 5ff9a0eadfe66b08
messages.subject: Fit meausures using sam function with multiple imputation (mitml)
parts:
Hi everyone I'm new here,

I'm trying to fit a sem model with 30 multiple-choice items developed to measure statistical reasoning in health science students as part of my phd thesis.  

I have three questions:

1) Because of the nature of the items and each item has only one correct answer I created 27 dummy variables to analyze the data in the sem models. Is this approach correct or do I have to use the 30 original items? All 27 dummy items are categorical, most of them are binary (0 if wrong and 1 if right, but only 6 items have three values (0, 0.5 and 1) because the 3 pairs of items were dependent in the sense of partial credit approach.  This is the model:

model2CB <- '
# Measurement model
problem=~ x1 + x2 + x3+ x4
analysis =~ x5+x6+x7+x8+ x9+x13+x14+x18+x19+x20+x21+x22+x23+x24
conclusions =~ x10+x11+x12+x15+x16+x17+x25+x26+x27

### Regressions

analysis ~ problem ## problem: exogenous
conclusions ~ problem + analysis

#Variances (1):
problem~~problem

#Factor errors  (2)
analysis~~analysis
conclusions~~conclusions
'

2) My sample size is small (149) and missing data is around 5%, so I wonder if is necessary to use multiple imputations here (I tested the original 30 items and Little's MCAR test reject, but when using the 27 dummy items, the same test is not significant) or pairwise would be enough. 

3)  In any case, I made multiple imputations with mice package(m=50 datasets), but because the with function in mice did not work with lavaan objects for the step analysis, I switched the imputed data from mice to mitml package (using the mids2mitml function):

library(mitml)

### To change from mids (x_imp1) to mid.mllist object:

x_imp.mitml<-mids2mitml.list(x_imp1) 

Then, with the imputed data in mitml package, I run sem model with all 50 data sets ( I decided to use the sam function in lavaan because of the sample size):

fit2_cb.sam <- with(x_imp.mitml,sam(model =model2CB , estimator = "wlsmv",ordered=T,check.gradient=F),include.data = TRUE).

The model converged and there were no warnings with any imputation:

[[1]] This is lavaan 0.6.16 -- using the SAM approach to SEM SAM method LOCAL Mapping matrix M method ML Number of measurement blocks 3 Estimator measurement part DWLS Estimator structural part ML Number of observations 149

I also pooled the results to obtain parameter estimates (within mitml package):

testEstimates(fit2_cb.sam,extra.pars = T)

However, I couldn't obtain the fit measures for the model fit2_cb.sam becuase the miml package does not have a summary function for that purpose (and considering that the fit objetct is not a lavaan object:

class(fit2_cb.sam) [1] "mitml.result" "list"

I cannot use lavaan or semTools functions, unless I do so for each of the 50 listresults. Or do you have any suggestions on how to manage the sam function with multiple imputations? ( I tried also the semTools package, but it only allowed me to use sem.Mi () function).

Thanks for any advice

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Fit meausures using sam function with multiple imputation (mitml)
parts: 1) Because of the nature of the items and each item has only one correct answer I created 27 dummy variables to analyze the data in the sem models. Is this approach correct or do I have to use the 30 original items? All 27 dummy items are categorical, most of them are binary (0 if wrong and 1 if right, but only 6 items have three values (0, 0.5 and 1) because the 3 pairs of items were dependent in the sense of partial credit approach.

If "partially correct" is a category between "not at all correct" and "fully correct", then you need to have a single ordinal variable coded that way.  The numerical values are arbitrary, as long as the order is recognized by lavaan.  You could use the ordered() function to make the levels explicit.

2) My sample size is small (149) and missing data is around 5%, so I wonder if is necessary to use multiple imputations here (I tested the original 30 items and Little's MCAR test reject, but when using the 27 dummy items, the same test is not significant) or pairwise would be enough.

MCAR is the null hypothesis.  It can be falsified by the data, but failing to reject is an inconclusive result.  There is no way to "verify" MCAR.  Imputation is often the most flexible way to include as many potentially informative auxiliary variables in your data to help justify the MAR assumption.  But there is nothing wrong with a sensitivity analysis, if you want to compare using missing="pairwise", potentially with estimator="PML".

3)  I couldn't obtain the fit measures for the model fit2_cb.sam

The chi-squared for SAM is a "pseudo" statistic that treats the "stage 1" saturated factor covariances as known.  As the article states (see ?sam References), the purpose of SAM is to make parameter estimation a bit more efficient, not to test model fit.
I tried also the semTools package, but it only allowed me to use sem.Mi () function

I have not written a sam.mi() wrapper, nor do I intend to.  (A valid implementation would do all the pooling of the measurement results, then fit the structural model to the pooled latent covariance matrix.  But that has not been developed, and many details would need to be worked out first.)  

I would recommend doing what you already did with mitml on fitted sam() results.  Just focus on pooled estimates, not the fit (pseudo)statistic.  Again, you could compare results to pairwise deletion as a sensitivity analysis.  If parameter estimates and SEs are similar, you could perhaps trust the fit statistic using pairwise deletion.
